No test added to verify the data race fix

The PR fixes a data race on the global `entryPointAssetsCache` variable by introducing `entryPointAssetsCacheMu`, but no test (e.g., one exercised with `go test -race` under concurrent calls to `GetWebAssets`) was added to validate the fix or guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could reintroduce the race undetected by CI unless the race detector happens to catch it in another path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Confusing dead-code logic in enableSqlExpressions makes the security gate fragile

The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the inverted naming — `enabled` actually means 'feature flag is NOT set') and then has an `if enabled { return false }` followed by an unconditional `return false`. Both branches return `false`, so the function always disables SQL expressions regardless of the feature-flag state — which is presumably the intent (to patch the RCE/LFI vulnerability), but the code reads as if it is supposed to check the flag and enable the feature when set. This is highly confusing: a future maintainer looking at this code will likely 'fix' the apparent dead branch/unused logic, assuming it's a bug, and could inadvertently re-enable the vulnerable SQL-expression execution path. Given this function is the primary gate preventing exploitation of the CVE, it should be a single explicit `return false` with a clear comment explaining why SQL expressions are permanently disabled, not an inverted boolean with unreachable branches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub error messages ('not implemented') obscure that the feature is intentionally and permanently disabled for security reasons

All methods on the new stub `DB` type (`TablesList`, `RunCommands`, `QueryFramesInto`) return a generic `errors.New("not implemented")`. Combined with the feature-flag check that also always disables SQL expressions, this gives operators/support staff no indication that the feature was intentionally and permanently removed due to a security vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264) rather than simply unfinished. This can lead to confusing support tickets or well-meaning future attempts to 'finish implementing' the stub, inadvertently reopening the vulnerability if not accompanied by a code comment or clearer error message explaining the deliberate removal.

false_positives.candidate:
Leftover 'duckDB' variable name contradicts PR's stated goal to remove DuckDB references

The PR description states the goal is to 'Remove reference to DuckDB', but `TablesList` still assigns `duckDB := NewInMemoryDB()`, keeping a DuckDB-specific variable name even though the underlying DuckDB dependency (`scottlepp/go-duck`) has been removed and replaced by the stub `DB` struct. This is a minor but visible inconsistency with the PR's own description and could confuse future readers into thinking a DuckDB engine is still in use.

No tests added/updated verifying SQL expressions are now blocked

The PR introduces a security-critical change (fully disabling SQL expression execution via `enableSqlExpressions` and stubbing out the SQL engine) but does not add or update any tests in `pkg/expr` to assert that: (1) `ReadQuery` returns the 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' error for `QueryTypeSQL` regardless of feature flag state, and (2) `SQLCommand.Execute`/`NewSQLCommand` fail safely now that `sql.TablesList`/`QueryFramesInto` always return errors. Without such tests, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the vulnerable code path (e.g., by 'fixing' the dead logic in `enableSqlExpressions`) without any test catching the regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the whole-function lock in BuildIndex allows duplicate concurrent builds for the same key

Previously `BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire duration, which (as a side effect) serialized all builds, including duplicate builds for the same `NamespacedResource` key. Now the lock is only taken when writing the final result into `b.cache` (lines 137-139). If two callers (e.g. two concurrent requests to `getOrCreateIndex`) trigger a build for the same key before either completes, both will independently build a full index (including, for file-backed indexes, opening/writing to the same directory via `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` at line 98), and only the last one to finish 'wins' the cache slot — the other built index is silently discarded without being closed, leaking memory/file handles, and the two concurrent file-based bleve.New calls on the same directory can also conflict/fail. There is no key-level locking (the existing TODO at the top of getOrCreateIndex acknowledges this), so this PR's removal of the broader lock increases the chance of this duplicate-build race actually occurring under load.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs() reads the cache map without holding cacheMu, racing with concurrent writers

`TotalDocs()` iterates over `b.cache` (line 146) without acquiring `cacheMu` (not even RLock), while `BuildIndex` and other paths write to the same map under `cacheMu.Lock()`. This is an unsynchronized concurrent map access, which can produce a 'concurrent map read and map write' runtime panic if `TotalDocs()` is called (e.g., from metrics scraping or from `searchSupport.init()`'s log line at the end of initialization) while another goroutine is still building/caching an index. The PR's stated goal of enabling more concurrent index building increases the odds of this race being hit in practice.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared `err` variable across concurrent goroutines in search index init

Inside `searchSupport.init()`, multiple goroutines spawned via `group.Go(...)` all read and write the single shared `err` variable declared outside the loop (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and then `return err`. Because the assignment and the `return` are two separate statements, one goroutine's assignment can be overwritten by another goroutine's assignment before its own `return err` executes, causing errgroup to receive the wrong goroutine's result (potentially losing a real build error, or reporting an unrelated one). This is also a plain data race flagged by `go test -race`. This bug is now far more consequential because `init()` is invoked synchronously during `NewResourceServer`, directly gating process startup — an incorrect/lost error here can mask a failed index build or incorrectly fail startup.

Postgres integration test skipped without root-causing a likely regression from this PR

The test `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` is now skipped for postgres with the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This test exercises exactly the module-server startup path that this PR changes (ResourceServer now blocks on Init() synchronously at construction instead of lazily). It's very plausible the test now fails/times out because startup takes longer or behaves differently with the new eager initialization, and the fix should be to address the underlying timing/behavior rather than silently skip the only integration test covering this startup path for a specific backend.

Resource server construction now blocks indefinitely with no timeout on index build

NewResourceServer() calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously before returning, and `ctx` here is derived from `context.WithCancel(context.Background())` with no deadline. If building the search index (or any lifecycle hook) takes a very long time or hangs (e.g. due to a slow/unavailable DB), NewResourceServer will never return, blocking the whole process startup indefinitely with no way to time out or recover. Previously this work happened lazily on the first gRPC call, so a slow index build at least allowed the server/process to start and expose health endpoints; now the entire service construction is gated on this unbounded operation. This directly matches the question raised in the PR description about what could break by making init eager, and should be addressed with a startup timeout/cancellation strategy or by running Init in the background with a readiness gate.

Unsynchronized increment of totalBatchesIndexed across goroutines

`totalBatchesIndexed++` is incremented inside each `group.Go` closure, i.e. concurrently from multiple goroutines (bounded by `initWorkers`), with no mutex or atomic operation. This is a data race that can produce an incorrect count used in the subsequent `span.AddEvent` call, and will be flagged by Go's race detector. Given this PR's goal of increasing indexing concurrency, this latent race becomes more likely to actually manifest/be hit by the race detector in CI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.
Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

false_positives.candidate:
Asymmetric isEnabled() evaluation between original and updated model in login invalidation check

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated) is called from update() with `original` being the result of getById(), which wraps the model through createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel (its isEnabled() depends dynamically on the linked organization's current enabled state). The `updated` parameter, however, is the raw model passed into update() and uses the static isEnabled() field value. When the organization is currently disabled, getLoginPredicate().test(original) and getLoginPredicate().test(updated) can diverge purely due to this wrapping difference rather than due to an actual change in the IDP, leading to unnecessary cache invalidations. While this does not appear to cause stale caches (it only triggers extra invalidation), the asymmetry is inconsistent and could mask more serious issues if the wrapping logic changes in the future.

Login cache invalidation is always applied to all three fetch modes, causing cache thrashing for multi-organization realms

registerIDPLoginInvalidation() and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() always invalidate the cache keys for all three FetchMode values (REALM_ONLY, ORG_ONLY, ALL) whenever any IDP crosses login-eligibility, regardless of which organization (if any) is actually affected. Unlike getByOrganization(), which caches/invalidates per specific organization id (cacheKeyOrgId), the getForLogin() cache stores results for ALL organizations' queries inside a single IdentityProviderListQuery keyed only by realm+mode. This means a single IDP update unrelated to a particular organization wipes out cached login results for every organization in the realm, causing unnecessary cache misses and re-queries in realms with many organizations.

No test coverage for the isEnabled() re-check fix introduced in the login IDP bean

This PR adds `idp.isEnabled()` re-checks in searchForIdentityProviders() for the ORG_ONLY and ALL branches, specifically to handle the case where a cached IDP model is wrapped and its effective isEnabled() depends on live organization enablement status that may differ from what was cached. No test was added (in OrganizationCacheTest or elsewhere) that exercises this specific scenario, e.g. disabling an organization after the login IDP list has been cached and verifying that disabled-org IDPs are filtered out of the rendered login page bean. Without such a test, a regression in this filtering logic (e.g. someone removing the re-check) would not be caught.

Public static predicate semantics changed without versioning/compat note

LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() is a public static method on a server-spi interface, and its behavior has been changed to additionally require that organization-linked IDPs have BROKER_PUBLIC=true. Any existing external code (custom providers, extensions) that already calls this public API expecting the old semantics (only ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN checks) will now silently get different results. Since server-spi is a public extension point, this behavior change should be called out explicitly (e.g., in release notes or javadoc) as it is a backward-incompatible semantic change to a public method, not just an internal implementation detail.

Single cache entry per mode can accumulate unbounded per-organization result sets

getForLogin() caches results under a single key per FetchMode (cacheKeyForLogin), with per-organization result sets stored inside the same IdentityProviderListQuery object (keyed internally by organizationId as the search key). In realms with many organizations, repeated getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, orgId) calls for different organizations will keep adding entries to the same cached object indefinitely, since there is no per-org eviction — only a full invalidation of the whole mode-level entry. This can lead to unbounded growth of a single cache entry in multi-tenant/many-organization deployments.

remove() now always performs an extra storage lookup

In remove(), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now executed unconditionally before checking `isInvalid(cacheKey)`. Previously, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was only invoked inside the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch; when the cache entry was valid, the code relied solely on the already-cached `CachedIdentityProvider` without hitting the underlying storage. With this change, every call to remove() now performs an unconditional read against the delegate storage provider (JPA), even when a valid cached copy is already available, just to determine whether to invalidate the login caches. This is a measurable regression on a hot path (IDP removal) and could have been avoided by reusing the already-fetched `cached.getIdentityProvider()` when present.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() does not actually return a BouncyCastle provider

The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. whatever JCA provider backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically the JDK's built-in provider, not BouncyCastle). This contradicts the documented contract of the method ("BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider") and is misleading for any caller (e.g. via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER in the common module) that assumes the returned provider name/behavior matches a BC-compatible provider. This could cause obscure NoSuchProviderException or incorrect algorithm resolution wherever generic code paths (not overridden with UnsupportedOperationException in this class) rely on this provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead/leftover code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) whose results are discarded and have no effect on the method's output - the actual DER sequence is built again right afterwards on lines 117-121. This is clearly leftover debugging/refactoring code that should be removed; it wastes allocations and makes the method harder to review/maintain.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks binary/source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI interface. Adding `int order();` as a plain abstract method (no default implementation) means any third-party or external implementation of CryptoProvider that does not implement order() will fail to compile/load (AbstractMethodError at runtime for compiled classes). Since CryptoProvider is loaded via ServiceLoader and is explicitly designed to allow multiple implementations on the classpath (per this PR's own rationale), existing external providers will break. A default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve backward compatibility while still allowing the new ordering feature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Inconsistent use of format.name() instead of format.toString() for KeyStore lookup

getKeyStore() calls `KeyStore.getInstance(format.name())`, whereas every other CryptoProvider implementation in this PR (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) consistently uses `format.toString()`. If KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat overrides toString() to return a value different from the enum constant name() (which is a common pattern for such enums, e.g. to map to the exact JCA keystore type string), this implementation will request a different/incorrect keystore type than intended, potentially throwing KeyStoreException at runtime for formats where name() and toString() diverge.

Multiple-provider conflict is now silently resolved instead of failing fast

Previously, detecting more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath threw an IllegalStateException, forcing the user to fix a misconfigured/ambiguous classpath. Now the code silently picks the provider with the highest order() value and only logs the ignored ones at debug level (which is often disabled in production). If two providers happen to have the same order() value (e.g. DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider both return 200), the selection becomes non-deterministic (dependent on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order), which can silently select the wrong crypto backend (e.g., non-FIPS instead of FIPS) without any error, which is a serious regression for environments that require strict crypto provider guarantees.

No test coverage for the new provider-ordering/selection logic

The detectProvider() method's behavior changed significantly: it now sorts providers by order() and silently picks the highest, logging the rest. There is no unit test added in this PR verifying that, given multiple CryptoProvider implementations with different order() values on the classpath, the correct (highest-order) one is selected, nor a test for the tie-break behavior when two providers share the same order(). This is core logic for the stated goal of the PR (allowing multiple CryptoProvider instances) and should be covered by a dedicated test.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup listener for removed clients/roles/groups is now skipped entirely when only V2 admin permissions are enabled

The ProviderEventListener body (handling RoleContainerModel.RoleRemovedEvent, ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent, GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent) is now wrapped in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`, i.e. it only runs for the legacy V1 feature. Previously it ran unconditionally. This change appears necessary because, under V2, ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled/isPermissionsEnabled throw UnsupportedOperationException, which would otherwise crash on every client removal when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. However, by gating the whole handler behind the V1 flag instead of adding an equivalent V2 cleanup path, no corresponding cleanup of V2 authorization resources happens when a client, role, or group is deleted while only V2 is enabled. This leaves orphaned 'Clients'/'Users' resources and related policies referencing deleted entities in the authorization store, a data-integrity regression with no compensating implementation added in this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission queries resources by type, but per-client resources are created without their type being set

getClientsWithPermission() calls resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) to enumerate per-client resources. However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() (server-spi-private/.../AdminPermissionsSchema.java) creates the individual client resource via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId()) and only calls resource.updateScopes(...); it never calls resource.setType(resourceType). Only the pre-created 'all-resource' resources built in init() have their type explicitly set. Unless the resource type is populated some other way, findByType will not match the individual per-client resources, so getClientsWithPermission() would return an incomplete/incorrect result (at best only the 'all-clients' aggregate resource, whose name is the literal string 'Clients', not a real client id).

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NullPointerException risk when the 'Clients' all-resource type resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when no per-client resource exists, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking whether the returned resource is null. getResourceTypeResource can legitimately return null (e.g. unsupported schema, or the 'Clients' resource not yet created for pre-existing admin-permission realms, see the related init() migration gap). Passing a null resource into findByResource is very likely to throw an NPE in the underlying store implementation, causing permission evaluation (canManage, canConfigure, canView, canMapRoles, etc. for a specific client) to fail with an unhandled exception instead of gracefully denying access.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
New CLIENTS resource type/scopes are never created for realms that already have an admin-permissions client

init() only performs the full setup (creating scopes and the per-resource-type 'all-resource' resources, including the newly added CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE scopes CONFIGURE/MANAGE/MAP_ROLES/MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE/MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE/VIEW and the 'Clients' resource) when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is null; otherwise it returns immediately (lines 226-228). Any realm that already enabled ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 before this PR already has a non-null admin permissions client, so after upgrading, init() will no-op for that realm and the new 'Clients' scopes/resource will never be created. As a result the whole new Clients permission feature is silently non-functional (and, combined with the missing null-check described elsewhere, can throw NPEs) for any realm that adopted V2 admin permissions prior to this change. There is no migration logic added to retrofit the new resource type/scopes into already-provisioned admin-permission resource servers.

Roles created in testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient are not cleaned up

This test creates a client role ('myclient-role') and a sub-role ('myclient-subRole') directly via the admin API but, unlike similar tests elsewhere in this PR (e.g. UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.testMapRoles, which registers realm.cleanup().add(...) for the created role), it registers no cleanup. If the managed realm/test fixtures are reused across test methods in this class, the created roles and their composite relationship will persist beyond the test, which can affect subsequent tests or leave stale data.

canList() javadoc references QUERY_USERS role which is unrelated to listing clients

The newly added javadoc for canList() states: 'Or if the caller has at least one of the AdminRoles#QUERY_CLIENTS or AdminRoles#QUERY_USERS roles.' This appears to be a copy/paste mistake from the analogous Users permission evaluator documentation; QUERY_USERS has no obvious relation to listing clients and is likely to mislead readers about the actual authorization requirements for this method.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

The update-compatibility command (and its exit codes) were already documented/shipped as a preview feature before this PR. Any automation or CI scripts already built against the prior exit code (4 == recreate required) will now get a different, misleading result: exit code 4 now means 'feature disabled' instead of 'recreate needed', and exit code 3 now means what 4 used to mean. This silently changes the contract of a tool meant to be consumed by scripts/pipelines, which is explicitly called out in the docs as a GitOps-friendly, scriptable tool.

Since this PR also changes which numeric exit code is used for 'recreate' vs 'feature disabled' (3 vs 4), a future regression that swaps these codes again would not be caught by this test even though the exit code is the primary machine-readable contract of this command per the documentation.

No negative test for rolling-updates feature being disabled on the operator

The updated test only exercises the scenario where the 'rolling-updates' feature is enabled via FeatureSpec. The newly-added documentation (docs/guides/operator/advanced-configuration.adoc) explicitly states in a CAUTION block that 'While on preview stage, the feature rolling-updates must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() for Groups grants management rights with only VIEW scope

GroupPermissionsV2#canManage() (no-arg) calls hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) - exactly the same call used by canManage()'s sibling canView(). This means a caller who was only granted the VIEW scope on the all-groups ('Groups') resource (and not MANAGE) will have canManage() return true. Since GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() and other mutating endpoints call auth.groups().requireManage(), a user with view-only permission on groups can create/modify top-level groups, which is a privilege escalation. Compare with canManage(GroupModel) in the same file which correctly only checks AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE. The no-arg canManage() should only check the MANAGE scope, not VIEW+MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses Resource.getId() instead of Resource.getName() when looking up/collecting group IDs

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the lambda passed to resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) receives Resource objects whose 'name' field holds the actual Group ID (per AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource/resolveGroup, which creates the resource with name=group.getId()). The code instead uses groupResource.getId() (the Resource entity's own internal id) both as the key passed into hasPermission(groupId, ...) - which does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) - and as the value added to the 'granted' set. Because the Resource's internal id generally does not equal the group id used as the resource name, the findByName lookup fails for every resource, hasPermission() falls back to checking only the 'all-groups' permission (which is usually absent in the per-group-permission scenario), and the returned set either stays empty or (worse) contains bogus resource IDs rather than real group IDs. This breaks group-scoped user visibility/search (UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource rely on these IDs to filter users by group membership), and should make the newly added GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest#testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers/testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers tests fail or behave incorrectly. false_positives.candidate:
Per-subgroup canView() re-evaluation replaces a cached global check

getSubGroups() previously computed `boolean canViewGlobal = auth.groups().canView();` once and used `.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || auth.groups().canView(g))`, so when the caller already has global view rights, no further permission evaluation was performed per subgroup. The change to `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)` calls canView(GroupModel) for every subgroup, and that method internally re-invokes canView() (role check, and for V2 FGAP a full authorization policy evaluation) for every single element. For realms with many subgroups and FGAP V2 enabled, this turns one policy evaluation into N policy evaluations per request, which is a real performance regression. The same pattern was also introduced in GroupsResource.getGroups().

Public utility method removed without deprecation

The public static method `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes(KeycloakSession, RealmModel, Map<String,String>, Integer, Integer)` was removed entirely (its one-line body was simply inlined into GroupsResource). Since this is a public static method on a widely-used utility class, any external code (custom providers/extensions) calling it directly will fail to compile/link against the new version. If this method is intended to be internal-only, it should at least be deprecated before removal rather than removed outright in the same change.

getResourceName() not extended for the new Groups resource type

getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE to return a friendly label ('All users') for the all-users resource and the username for individual user resources, but no equivalent branch was added for GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE even though this PR introduces Groups as a full resource type with the same 'all-resource vs individual resource (named by id)' pattern. As a result, scope permissions for groups will fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), which for group resources is just the raw group id/UUID rather than a readable group name or an 'All groups' label, unlike the symmetric handling added for Users.

Translations that legitimately reorder anchor tags (common due to different grammar/word order) will trigger a false 'Didn't find anchor tag' verification failure even though the same tags are present, just in a different order, causing legitimate translations to fail CI/build verification.

Fragile, unguarded derivation of the English reference file path

The English counterpart file path is derived purely via two chained `String.replaceAll` calls on the absolute path (`resources-community`->`resources`, and the locale suffix ->`_en.properties`). If this heuristic fails to produce an existing file (e.g. non-standard directory layouts, or a locale file whose English source doesn't live where the heuristic expects), the subsequent `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` throws an IOException that is converted into an uncaught RuntimeException (see other finding), crashing the whole verification run instead of reporting a specific, actionable error for that file.

HTML detection regex misses uppercase and closing tags `HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` only matches lowercase opening tags. English source strings whose only HTML markers are closing tags (e.g. ``) or use uppercase tag names will be judged as not containing HTML by containsHtml(), causing the stricter POLICY_NO_HTML to be applied to translations even when the English source itself is HTML-bearing, which can produce confusing or incorrect verification results.

Lithuanian login translation replaced with Italian text

The key `loginTotpStep1` for the Lithuanian login theme was changed to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian text, not a Lithuanian translation. This is the same mistake as in the account theme's `messages_lt.properties` and will show Lithuanian users an Italian sentence on the TOTP setup screen.

No tests for normalizeValue special-case branches or the happy-path (valid translation) scenario

normalizeValue() contains several non-trivial special-case branches (templateHelp's `CLAIM.<NAME>` allowance, optimizeLookupHelp's `<Extensions>` allowance, linkExpirationFormatter/error-invalid-multivalued-size ChoiceFormat stripping, and email RTL style stripping), none of which are covered by any test. There is also no test confirming that a well-formed translation containing legitimate allowed HTML/anchors passes verification without reporting any messages, so regressions in these code paths (e.g. the i18next-breaking change found in account-ui/admin-ui files) would not be caught by this test suite.

i18next placeholder syntax broken by Java-style MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat substitution

This file is consumed by the React account-ui app via react-i18next, which requires double-curly-brace interpolation syntax (`{{0}}`). The change replaces `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` with `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`, which uses single braces and Java's MessageFormat ChoiceFormat syntax. i18next will not interpret `{0}` as a variable and has no understanding of `{2,choice,...}`, so this message will render literally/unsubstituted (or broken) in the Account Console UI instead of being correctly interpolated. The same regression is applied to the admin-ui translation file.

Same issue as in account-ui: `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` was changed to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. This file is consumed by the React admin-ui through react-i18next, which uses `{{var}}` double-brace syntax, not Java MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat. The new text will not be correctly interpolated in the Admin Console, showing raw/unsubstituted template text to users.

verifySafeHtml throws unchecked RuntimeException instead of the declared MojoExecutionException

verify() declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and only catches IOException from the duplicate-key check, but verifySafeHtml() wraps its own IOExceptions (reading the file or the derived English reference file) in `RuntimeException`. These RuntimeExceptions are not caught anywhere in verify(), so they propagate uncaught out of the public API, producing an unhandled exception/raw stack trace during the Maven build instead of the clean MojoExecutionException the method contract promises, and aborting the whole verification run rather than reporting it as a verification failure for that file.

`isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)` is supposed to assert that the 4th/5th characters of the encoded token-id context equal the expected grant-type shortcut (as the comment above states, chars 4-5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`). Instead: (1) it uses `substring(3, 5)` which is the wrong character range (off-by-one, grabs the last char of the token-type shortcut plus the first char of the grant-type shortcut), and (2) the condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no match) precisely when the substring equals the expected value, and otherwise falls through to only check that the raw id portion is a UUID, effectively ignoring the grant-type shortcut entirely. This means `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` (all of which rely on this matcher) will fail when the grant shortcut is actually correct, and will incorrectly pass when it is wrong, defeating the purpose of the added assertion and potentially causing spurious CI failures or false-positive test passes.

This is a stricter contract than the previous 'any string is a valid token id' assumption, and has no fallback path for ids that incidentally contain a colon but aren't 6-char-shortcut encoded.

On platforms/configurations where the *default* multiprocessing context is not spawn (e.g. fork on Linux, which is Sentry's typical deployment target), `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to a different class (e.g. `ForkProcess`), and `isinstance(spawn_process, multiprocessing.Process)` evaluates to False. Previously (pre-PR) `kill()` was called unconditionally, so this guard is new and can silently prevent an unhealthy/hung child process from ever being killed before a replacement process is spawned for the same shards. The result is two processes concurrently flushing/producing the same shard's segments, risking duplicate production to the buffered-segments topic (data integrity) and leaked/zombie OS processes.

These RuntimeExceptions are not caught anywhere in verify(), so they propagate uncaught out of the public API, producing an unhandled exception/raw stack trace during the Maven build instead of the clean MojoExecutionException the method contract promises, and aborting the whole verification run rather than reporting it as a verification failure for that file.

New abstract method getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a public extension SPI (used to plug in custom OAuth2 grant types). This PR adds a new abstract method `String getShortcut();` with no default implementation. Any existing third-party/custom implementation of this SPI will fail to compile or fail provider loading until it implements this new method, which is a backward-incompatible API change for an SPI explicitly intended to be extensible (as mentioned in the PR description itself). A default method (e.g. returning a generated/fallback shortcut) would avoid breaking existing providers.

getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut dereference sessionFactory without a null check, causing NPE instead of a clear error

`getShortcutByGrantType()` (line 110) and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` (line 125) use `sessionFactory` to refresh the shortcut maps when a lookup misses, but `sessionFactory` is only assigned in `postInit()`. If these methods are invoked on an instance where `postInit()` has not run (e.g. unusual initialization ordering, or direct instantiation as done in the accompanying unit test), a NullPointerException is thrown instead of the intended, user-facing `IllegalArgumentException`/`IllegalStateException` for unknown shortcuts/grant types. This makes failure diagnosis harder in edge cases and indicates the methods should defensively check for a null `sessionFactory`.

Access token 'jti' is no longer an opaque random UUID; no backward-compatibility note or opt-out

`initToken()` now builds the access token id via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)`, producing ids like `onrtac:1f65761e-...` instead of a plain UUID as before. External tooling, log parsers, audit systems, or custom code relying on the `jti` claim being a canonical UUID (fixed length/format) will break after upgrading. The PR introduces no migration notes, deprecation warning, or configuration flag to retain the previous plain-UUID behavior for users who depend on the old format, which is a user-facing behavioral/API change for a widely consumed token claim.

Decoding logic unconditionally treats any colon-containing token id as encoded context, risking false failures for unrelated legacy ids

`getTokenContextFromTokenId()` treats the presence of a ':' anywhere in the token id as indicating the new context-encoded format, then requires the prefix to be exactly 6 characters matching known shortcuts, throwing `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise. If any pre-existing or externally generated token id (not produced by this encoder) happens to contain a ':' for unrelated reasons, this method will throw a hard error instead of gracefully treating the whole string as a raw/legacy id (as is done for ids without a colon). This is a stricter contract than the previous 'any string is a valid token id' assumption, and has no fallback path for ids that incidentally contain a colon but aren't 6-char-shortcut encoded.

Use of queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown requires Python 3.13+

Both `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were only added in Python 3.13. If Sentry's runtime is on an earlier Python version (3.11/3.12, which is common for this codebase), `q.shutdown()` will raise `AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'`, which is silently swallowed by the broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` in `shutdown()`. As a result, worker threads will never receive a shutdown signal and will hang forever blocked on `work_queue.get()`, making graceful shutdown completely non-functional and leaking daemon threads for the life of the process.

Queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure guarantee

`work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `FixedQueuePool.submit()`/`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never block on a full queue. The class docstrings claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up,' but since the queue is unbounded, a single slow group assigned to a queue will cause that queue (and thus memory usage) to grow without limit while the main consumer thread keeps consuming and submitting new items. This defeats the stated goal of this PR (avoiding unbounded backlog from slow items) and risks unbounded memory growth under sustained slow processing.

Sequential worker joins on shutdown can take far longer than expected

In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, `for worker in self.workers: worker.join(timeout=5.0)` joins each worker thread sequentially with a 5 second timeout. With the default `num_queues=20`, a slow shutdown could take up to 20 * 5 = 100 seconds in the worst case. This can exceed typical process termination grace periods (e.g. Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`), resulting in SIGKILL before threads finish, undermining the goal of a graceful shutdown and risking lost/duplicated in-flight work.

queue_pool is permanently nulled on shutdown, breaking subsequent create_with_partitions calls

`ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` sets `self.queue_pool = None` after calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but `self.thread_queue_parallel` stays `True` and the pool is never recreated. If `create_with_partitions()` is invoked again on this factory instance after `shutdown()` is called (e.g. during a partition rebalance or any lifecycle path where the strategy factory outlives individual strategy instances), `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will hit `assert self.queue_pool is not None` and raise an AssertionError, crashing the consumer. The other modes (`parallel`, `batched-parallel`) don't exhibit this exact null-out pattern on their pools/executors.

Kafka offset commit invoked from a background thread, not the main poll loop

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` runs on a dedicated daemon thread (`self.commit_thread`) and periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ultimately drives the arroyo `Commit` callback tied to the underlying Kafka consumer. The underlying confluent-kafka-python/librdkafka client is documented as not safe for concurrent calls across threads (e.g. concurrent `poll()` from the main stream processor loop and `commit()`-related calls from this background thread). Introducing a separate thread that periodically triggers commits concurrently with the main consumer loop's polling is a new concurrency risk that did not exist for the other (serial/batched-parallel/parallel) modes, which all perform commits from the strategy pipeline on the main processing thread.

WorkItem retains the full Kafka Message object though it is never used

`WorkItem` stores the entire `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` (set in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`), but neither `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` nor any other code path reads `work_item.message` — only `partition`, `offset`, and `result` are used. Keeping a reference to the full raw Kafka message for every queued item unnecessarily increases memory retained by backlogged queues, especially since the queues are unbounded (see related finding), compounding potential memory pressure under backlog.

New thread-queue-parallel tests are tightly coupled to the 1-second commit loop timing

Tests such as `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit` and `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` poll for up to ~2 seconds (20 iterations of `time.sleep(0.1)`) waiting for a commit to appear, while `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` only attempts a commit once per second (`self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`). This leaves very little margin under CI load or thread scheduling delays, making these tests prone to intermittent flakiness rather than deterministically synchronizing on the commit event.

As a result, the derived child context used for the async Legacy write is very likely already canceled (or about to be) by the time the goroutine runs, causing the 'safety measure' legacy write to fail with context-canceled errors almost every time instead of actually mirroring data to legacy storage. Fallback locale translations are only pre-loaded inside ApplicationController requests, not in jobs/console/mailers

FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded! is only invoked from ApplicationController#set_locale (app/controllers/application_controller.rb line ~159). The actual lookup used by I18n::Backend::Fallbacks#translate calls `super(fallback, key, ...)` directly on the backend instance, bypassing the patched `I18n.translate` in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb that performs lazy `load_locale`. That means a fallback locale's YAML translations are only guaranteed to be loaded in memory when a web request goes through ApplicationController#set_locale beforehand. Any translation performed outside of a controller request lifecycle (Sidekiq jobs, mailers triggered from jobs, rake tasks, console) for a user whose locale differs from the default will not have the fallback locale(s) loaded, so a missing key in the user's locale will not actually fall back to the site default or English — it will just be reported as missing. This defeats the purpose of the fallback feature in exactly the contexts (async notifications/digests in minority locales) where it matters most.

No tests for the new fallback locale chain or load-triggering logic

This PR introduces a new FallbackLocaleList class that computes a fallback chain (user locale -> site default -> :en) and a new ensure_loaded! helper, plus a corresponding before_filter in ApplicationController. No specs were added to verify the fallback order, the dedup/compact behavior, that ensure_loaded! actually causes the expected locale files to load, or that end-to-end translation lookups correctly fall back when a key is missing in the primary locale. Given this is a behavior-changing feature (removing config.i18n.fallbacks = true and replacing it with custom logic), lack of test coverage risks silent regressions.

PR description provides no explanation of the change

The PR description is just "Test 9", with no explanation of why config.i18n.fallbacks was removed from three environment files in favor of a hand-rolled FallbackLocaleList, what the fallback chain semantics are, or what testing was performed. For a feature that changes global I18n fallback behavior and touches a performance-sensitive translation cache, reviewers and future maintainers have no context to evaluate correctness or intended behavior.

The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware (and its instrumentContext helper moved from the metrics middleware) has no dedicated test file added in this PR, even though it contains non-trivial logic for building contextual log attributes (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) per RPC method. Route param name mismatch breaks add_members / remove_member endpoints

`add_members` (line 66) and `remove_member` (line 85) call `params.require(:group_id)`, but the routes added in `config/routes.rb` (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` / `put "members" => "groups#add_members"`) are declared directly inside the `resources :groups do ... end` block without a `member do` wrapper or a custom `param:` option. Rails treats such bare routes as member routes using the resource's default id parameter, i.e. `:id` (same as `/admin/groups/:id`), not `:group_id`. As a result the real request path produces `params[:id]`, and `params.require(:group_id)` will raise `ActionController::ParameterMissing` for every real HTTP request made by the JS model's `addMembers`/`removeMember` calls (`Discourse.ajax('/admin/groups/' + this.get('id') + '/members.json', ...)`), making the core feature of this PR (adding/removing group members from the admin UI) non-functional in production.

The `.add_members` and `.remove_member` specs invoke the controller actions directly with `group_id: ...` (e.g. `xhr :put, :add_members, group_id: 1, usernames: "l77t"`). Rails' `ActionController::TestCase` dispatch bypasses real route recognition and just merges the given params, so these tests pass even though the actual routes (declared without a `member do` wrapper) would supply `:id` instead of `:group_id`. There is no request/integration spec exercising the real route, so the runtime `ParameterMissing` bug described separately is not caught by this test suite.

`{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}` likely uses wrong option name

The each-helper option for specifying a custom per-item view class in this version of Ember/Handlebars is `itemViewClass`, not `itemView` (as used consistently elsewhere in Discourse, e.g. `itemViewClass="..."`). Using `itemView` means the newly added `group-member` view/template (which renders the avatar, username and the remove-member link) will likely never be applied, so the admin group members list will not render as intended and the "remove member" UI added by this PR may simply not appear.

`{{#unless automatic}}` resolves against the wrong context, always showing remove link

This template is rendered as the item view for each member inside `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}`. Inside that per-item context, `automatic` is looked up on the member (a User) object, not on the outer group/controller, so it will always be undefined/false. Consequently `{{#unless automatic}}` always evaluates true and the "remove member" link is shown even for automatic groups, whose members cannot actually be removed (the server rejects such requests with a 422). This creates a confusing dead-end UI action instead of correctly hiding the control for automatic groups.

`app/controllers/groups_controller.rb#members` now always paginates with a default `limit` of 50 for every group (previously only automatic groups were capped, at 200, and regular groups returned the full member list). The public-facing `group/members.hbs` template has no next/previous controls (unlike the admin `group.hbs` template, which does), so any group with more than 50 members will silently show only the first 50 with no way to view the rest — a functional regression for larger groups.

The route now assigns the raw `Group` model object instead (`controller.set("model", model)`) and the template was changed to `{{#each m in members}}`. No controller file for group-members is included in this change set; if the existing controller is an `ArrayController` (as the prior code's usage suggests), assigning a non-array `Group` object as its content/model is likely to break member rendering on the public group page.

Untrusted RSS feed content is stored and rendered as raw HTML (stored XSS)

poll_feed.rb takes `i.content` straight from an externally-controlled RSS/Atom feed, only unescapes HTML entities, and passes it to `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)` with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` (see app/models/topic_embed.rb line 22). The embed view then outputs it unescaped (`<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb), and the normal topic page presumably does the same since `cooked` is generally trusted. A malicious or compromised feed can inject `<script>` tags or other active content that will execute in every visitor's browser (both on the embed page and on the main forum topic page). There is no sanitizer anywhere in this import path (Nokogiri's `absolutize_urls` only rewrites href/src, it doesn't strip scripts/attributes).

Use of Kernel#open (open-uri) on externally supplied URLs risks command/file injection

`import_remote` calls `open(url).read` (Kernel#open via `open-uri`) directly on a URL that is not scheme-validated before this point (the `^https?://` check only happens later, inside `TopicEmbed.import`, which `import_remote` never calls before opening the URL). `Kernel#open` is well known to treat strings beginning with a pipe character (e.g. `|some-shell-command`) as a command to execute, and can also open local files via `file://` or bare paths. `import_remote` is invoked directly with attacker/feed-influenced strings in `lib/tasks/disqus.thor` (`TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], ...)`, line 148) where `t[:link]` comes from parsing an externally supplied Disqus XML export, and in `lib/topic_retriever.rb#fetch_http` with the user-supplied `embed_url`. While `TopicRetriever#invalid_host?` provides some protection for the web-triggered path, the thor task has no such guard, and the scheme check inside `import_remote`→`import` happens too late (after `open` has already run). This should use a strict allow-list of schemes (http/https only) and/or `URI.open`/`Net::HTTP` instead of bare `Kernel#open` before performing the request.

Race condition on first-time embed import can raise unhandled RecordNotUnique

`TopicEmbed.import` checks `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` to decide whether to create a new topic/post or update an existing one. If two requests for the same new `embed_url` run concurrently (e.g. a user request and the hourly feed poller, or two near-simultaneous visitors before the Redis throttle key in `TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?` is set), both can see `embed.blank?` as true and both attempt `TopicEmbed.create!(...)` with the same `embed_url`. Since `embed_url` has a unique DB index (db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb), the second `create!` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`, which is not rescued anywhere in this path, causing the background job (or request) to fail with an unhandled exception instead of gracefully falling back to the update path.

No timeout on blocking HTTP fetch for feed polling (open-uri)

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses `open-uri` with no read/open timeout configured. If the configured feed URL is slow, unresponsive, or the connection hangs, this call can block the Sidekiq worker thread indefinitely (or for a very long time), since `sidekiq_options retry: false` won't help here and there is no `Timeout` wrapper. The same issue applies to `open(url).read` in `TopicEmbed#import_remote` (app/models/topic_embed.rb line 48). This can starve the scheduled-job queue of workers.

`feed_key` computes a Redis key based on a SHA1 of the feed URL (`"feed-modified:#{...}"`), presumably intended to support conditional GETs / tracking last-modified state to avoid re-downloading/re-parsing the whole feed on every run, but it is never referenced anywhere in `poll_feed` or elsewhere in the class. `require_dependency 'nokogiri'` loads the Nokogiri gem through Rails' autoload/dependency-tracking mechanism, which is meant for application code that should be reloaded between requests in development, not for third-party native-extension gems. Using `require_dependency` for a gem like Nokogiri is non-idiomatic and can cause Rails to attempt to track/reload it as part of the app's dependency graph, which is unnecessary overhead and can lead to subtle reload issues with native extensions. This should simply be `require 'nokogiri'` (or omitted entirely since Nokogiri is already a Bundler dependency loaded at boot).

When rescheduling, previous workflow reminders are cancelled via `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` with `immediateDelete=true`, which performs an immediate SendGrid 'scheduled_sends' cancel POST request synchronously (same mechanism described as the root cause of the original bug: too many pending cancellations accumulating and failing once the 100-pending-cancellation quota is hit). Unlike `handleCancelBooking.ts`, which now defers cancellation (sets `cancelled: true` and lets the cron job cancel close to send time), the reschedule flow does not benefit from this fix. Since the PR title explicitly claims to fix reminders for both cancelled AND rescheduled bookings, this inconsistency means the rescheduled-booking scenario can still hit the same SendGrid pending-cancellation limit and fail to cancel stale reminders.

A single failed SendGrid cancellation aborts cleanup of the entire cancellation batch

The for-loop over `remindersToCancel` performs the SendGrid cancel request and queues a DB delete for each reminder, but the whole loop (and the trailing `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)`) is wrapped in one try/catch. If the SendGrid request throws for any single reminder (e.g. transient network error, invalid/expired batch id), the exception propagates out of the loop immediately: remaining reminders in the batch are never processed in this run, and even reminders successfully cancelled with SendGrid earlier in the loop never get their DB delete executed (since `Promise.all` is never reached). This can cause workflow reminders to remain in a 'cancelled but not cleaned-up' state indefinitely if the failure recurs, and prevents other, unrelated reminders scheduled in the same cron tick from being cancelled at all this cycle.

remindersToCancel query lacks a method filter for EMAIL reminders

The query `prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: {...} } })` does not filter by `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. This endpoint (scheduleEmailReminders) subsequently treats every returned reminder's `referenceId` as a SendGrid `batch_id` and issues a SendGrid cancel request. If an SMS reminder (or any future reminder type) is ever marked `cancelled: true`, this cron job would incorrectly attempt to SendGrid-cancel it using a non-SendGrid reference id (e.g. a Twilio SID), causing an API error and, per the adjacent bug, potentially blocking cancellation of other legitimate email reminders in the same batch.

Unrelated UI refactor bundled into a backend bug-fix PR

This file's changes (merging the phone-number/sender-id blocks and removing the outer `(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded)` wrapper) are a UI refactor unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (fixing workflow reminders for cancelled/rescheduled bookings). While the change itself appears benign (it removes an effectively-empty wrapper div when only `isSenderIdNeeded` is true), bundling unrelated UI changes into a critical bug-fix PR makes the change harder to review and increases the risk of unintentionally introducing a UI regression that isn't covered by this PR's testing focus.

No automated tests cover the new deferred-cancellation / cron cancellation logic

This PR fixes a previously-reported production bug (workflow reminders still sent after cancellation/reschedule) by introducing a new `cancelled` flag and a batch cancellation step inside the `scheduleEmailReminders` cron job. No tests were added to verify that: (1) reminders marked `cancelled` within the 1-hour window are actually cancelled and removed, (2) a failure in one cancellation does not silently prevent cancellation of other reminders in the same run, or (3) the end-to-end flow (cancel booking -> cancelled flag set -> cron cancels in SendGrid) behaves as expected. Given this is explicitly fixing a reported bug, lack of regression tests risks the same issue resurfacing undetected.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

forEach callback made async but errors no longer caught by surrounding try/catch

However, `Array.prototype.forEach` never awaits the promises returned by its callback and does not propagate rejections to the caller. Previously the callback was synchronous, so any exception thrown inside it (e.g. from `getCalendar`) was thrown synchronously and caught by the surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { ... }` block. Now that the callback is async, any error (including a *synchronous* throw now wrapped into a rejected promise) becomes an unhandled promise rejection that bypasses the try/catch entirely. This both silently swallows/escapes expected error handling and means `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`/`deleteMeeting(...)` are fire-and-forget — the function can return before calendar/video cleanup actually completes.

The appStore object stores the results of calling `import("./x")` directly as object values, e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`. The test patches `time.sleep` globally at line 15 (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), which replaces the `sleep` attribute on the actual `time` module for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62, intended to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change," therefore does nothing — it resolves to the same monkeypatched no-op. The test's reliability against the race between updating `current_drift` and the background flusher thread observing it relies solely on incidental GIL/thread scheduling from the extra `step.poll()` call, not on any real wait, so the fix may not reliably prevent flakiness it was meant to address.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New isinstance guard can silently skip killing unhealthy multiprocessing flusher processes

In `_ensure_processes_alive()` the new code guards `process.kill()` with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process):`. The processes are actually created via `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so they are instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. On platforms/configurations where the *default* multiprocessing context is not spawn (e.g. fork on Linux, which is Sentry's typical deployment target), `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to a different class (e.g. `ForkProcess`), and `isinstance(spawn_process, multiprocessing.Process)` evaluates to False. Previously (pre-PR) `kill()` was called unconditionally, so this guard is new and can silently prevent an unhealthy/hung child process from ever being killed before a replacement process is spawned for the same shards. The result is two processes concurrently flushing/producing the same shard's segments, risking duplicate production to the buffered-segments topic (data integrity) and leaked/zombie OS processes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: flusher processes created with the spawn context are SpawnProcess instances that fail the multiprocessing.Process isinstance guard on POSIX, causing kill() to be skipped for hung processes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() aborts terminating remaining flusher processes once a deadline is hit mid-loop

In `join(timeout)`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` breaks out entirely as soon as the deadline is exceeded for the process currently being iterated (`if remaining_time <= 0: break`). This skips the `process.terminate()` call for all subsequent process indexes in the dict, not just the one that timed out. With a single flusher process (pre-PR behavior) this was not an issue, but with multiple flusher processes per shard group, hitting the timeout while waiting on an early process means later processes are never explicitly terminated during this shutdown path (e.g. during a strategy teardown/rebalance where the whole interpreter does not exit), leaving them running as orphaned subprocesses.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same shutdown bug: breaking out of the process loop when the deadline expires skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract method getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a public extension SPI (used to plug in custom OAuth2 grant types). This PR adds a new abstract method `String getShortcut();` with no default implementation. Any existing third-party/custom implementation of this SPI will fail to compile or fail provider loading until it implements this new method, which is a backward-incompatible API change for an SPI explicitly intended to be extensible (as mentioned in the PR description itself). A default method (e.g. returning a generated/fallback shortcut) would avoid breaking existing providers.

getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut dereference sessionFactory without a null check, causing NPE instead of a clear error

`getShortcutByGrantType()` (line 110) and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` (line 125) use `sessionFactory` to refresh the shortcut maps when a lookup misses, but `sessionFactory` is only assigned in `postInit()`. If these methods are invoked on an instance where `postInit()` has not run (e.g. unusual initialization ordering, or direct instantiation as done in the accompanying unit test), a NullPointerException is thrown instead of the intended, user-facing `IllegalArgumentException`/`IllegalStateException` for unknown shortcuts/grant types. This makes failure diagnosis harder in edge cases and indicates the methods should defensively check for a null `sessionFactory`.

Access token 'jti' is no longer an opaque random UUID; no backward-compatibility note or opt-out

`initToken()` now builds the access token id via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)`, producing ids like `onrtac:1f65761e-...` instead of a plain UUID as before. External tooling, log parsers, audit systems, or custom code relying on the `jti` claim being a canonical UUID (fixed length/format) will break after upgrading. The PR introduces no migration notes, deprecation warning, or configuration flag to retain the previous plain-UUID behavior for users who depend on the old format, which is a user-facing behavioral/API change for a widely consumed token claim.

Decoding logic unconditionally treats any colon-containing token id as encoded context, risking false failures for unrelated legacy ids

`getTokenContextFromTokenId()` treats the presence of a ':' anywhere in the token id as indicating the new context-encoded format, then requires the prefix to be exactly 6 characters matching known shortcuts, throwing `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise. If any pre-existing or externally generated token id (not produced by this encoder) happens to contain a ':' for unrelated reasons, this method will throw a hard error instead of gracefully treating the whole string as a raw/legacy id (as is done for ids without a colon). This is a stricter contract than the previous 'any string is a valid token id' assumption, and has no fallback path for ids that incidentally contain a colon but aren't 6-char-shortcut encoded.

If building the search index (or any lifecycle hook) takes a very long time or hangs (e.g. due to a slow/unavailable DB), NewResourceServer will never return, blocking the whole process startup indefinitely with no way to time out or recover. Previously this work happened lazily on the first gRPC call, so a slow index build at least allowed the server/process to start and expose health endpoints; now the entire service construction is gated on this unbounded operation. This directly matches the question raised in the PR description about what could break by making init eager, and should be addressed with a startup timeout/cancellation strategy or by running Init in the background with a readiness gate.

The test `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` is now skipped for postgres with the comment 'test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This test exercises exactly the module-server startup path that this PR changes (ResourceServer now blocks on Init() synchronously at construction instead of lazily). It's very plausible the test now fails/times out because startup takes longer or behaves differently with the new eager initialization, and the fix should be to address the underlying timing/behavior rather than silently skip the only integration test covering this startup path for a specific backend.

Data race on shared `err` variable across concurrent goroutines in search index init

Inside `searchSupport.init()`, multiple goroutines spawned via `group.Go(...)` all read and write the single shared `err` variable declared outside the loop (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and then `return err`. Because the assignment and the `return` are two separate statements, one goroutine's assignment can be overwritten by another goroutine's assignment before its own `return err` executes, causing errgroup to receive the wrong goroutine's result (potentially losing a real build error, or reporting an unrelated one). This is also a plain data race flagged by `go test -race`. This bug is now far more consequential because `init()` is invoked synchronously during `NewResourceServer`, directly gating process startup — an incorrect/lost error here can mask a failed index build or incorrectly fail startup.

Unsynchronized increment of totalBatchesIndexed across goroutines

`totalBatchesIndexed++` is incremented inside each `group.Go` closure, i.e. concurrently from multiple goroutines (bounded by `initWorkers`), with no mutex or atomic operation. This is a data race that can produce an incorrect count used in the subsequent `span.AddEvent` call, and will be flagged by Go's race detector. Given this PR's goal of increasing indexing concurrency, this latent race becomes more likely to actually manifest/be hit by the race detector in CI.

Use of queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown requires Python 3.13+

OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches `queue.ShutDown` (lines 132, 143) and FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` (line 238). Both `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were only added in Python 3.13. If Sentry's runtime is on an earlier Python version (3.11/3.12, which is common for this codebase), `q.shutdown()` will raise `AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown'`, which is silently swallowed by the broad `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` in `shutdown()`. As a result, worker threads will never receive a shutdown signal and will hang forever blocked on `work_queue.get()`, making graceful shutdown completely non-functional and leaking daemon threads for the life of the process.

Queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure guarantee

`work_queue: queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `FixedQueuePool.submit()`/`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never block on a full queue. The class docstrings claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up,' but since the queue is unbounded, a single slow group assigned to a queue will cause that queue (and thus memory usage) to grow without limit while the main consumer thread keeps consuming and submitting new items. This defeats the stated goal of this PR (avoiding unbounded backlog from slow items) and risks unbounded memory growth under sustained slow processing.

Sequential worker joins on shutdown can take far longer than expected

In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, `for worker in self.workers: worker.join(timeout=5.0)` joins each worker thread sequentially with a 5 second timeout. With the default `num_queues=20`, a slow shutdown could take up to 20 * 5 = 100 seconds in the worst case. This can exceed typical process termination grace periods (e.g. Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`), resulting in SIGKILL before threads finish, undermining the goal of a graceful shutdown and risking lost/duplicated in-flight work.

queue_pool is permanently nulled on shutdown, breaking subsequent create_with_partitions calls

`ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()` sets `self.queue_pool = None` after calling `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but `self.thread_queue_parallel` stays `True` and the pool is never recreated. If `create_with_partitions()` is invoked again on this factory instance after `shutdown()` is called (e.g. during a partition rebalance or any lifecycle path where the strategy factory outlives individual strategy instances), `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will hit `assert self.queue_pool is not None` and raise an AssertionError, crashing the consumer. The other modes (`parallel`, `batched-parallel`) don't exhibit this exact null-out pattern on their pools/executors.

Kafka offset commit invoked from a background thread, not the main poll loop

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` runs on a dedicated daemon thread (`self.commit_thread`) and periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ultimately drives the arroyo `Commit` callback tied to the underlying Kafka consumer. The underlying confluent-kafka-python/librdkafka client is documented as not safe for concurrent calls across threads (e.g. concurrent `poll()` from the main stream processor loop and `commit()`-related calls from this background thread). Introducing a separate thread that periodically triggers commits concurrently with the main consumer loop's polling is a new concurrency risk that did not exist for the other (serial/batched-parallel/parallel) modes, which all perform commits from the strategy pipeline on the main processing thread.

WorkItem retains the full Kafka Message object though it is never used

`WorkItem` stores the entire `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` (set in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`), but neither `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` nor any other code path reads `work_item.message` — only `partition`, `offset`, and `result` are used. Keeping a reference to the full raw Kafka message for every queued item unnecessarily increases memory retained by backlogged queues, especially since the queues are unbounded (see related finding), compounding potential memory pressure under backlog.
